name: Liposomal IGF-1

card.summary: IGF-1 in liposomes for the scalp; the biology is plausible on paper but evidence is preclinical.

quick.overview:
Liposomal IGF-1 is a topical idea: deliver the growth factor IGF-1 to hair follicles inside fat-like carriers.

IGF-1 is naturally produced in the follicle, but studies of the topical product in people were not found.
quick.mechanism: IGF-1 acts on dermal papilla cells, promoting growth-phase signalling through PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK. [1]
quick.risks: Safety of topical IGF-1 on the scalp has not been established in published trials; it is an unapproved product for hair.

lead: Liposomal IGF-1 is insulin-like growth factor 1 packaged in liposomes, tiny fat-based carriers, for application to the scalp. The aim is to deliver a growth signal to the hair follicle so that follicles stay longer in the growth phase, which in turn could support thicker, denser-looking hair. [1]

IGF-1 is a 70-amino-acid hormone made mainly by the liver in response to growth hormone. [3] In hair, it is made mainly by dermal papilla cells at the base of the follicle; a 2025 review describes it as acting through PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK signalling to promote follicle proliferation, inhibit apoptosis, extend the anagen (growth) phase and raise VEGF, which supports blood supply to the follicle. [1][2] The same review reports that IGF-1 and VEGF are lower in dermal papilla cells in androgenetic alopecia. [2]

The liposomal gel format has been tested in animals: a 2012 hamster study by Castro and colleagues used 1% and 3% liposomal IGF-1 gels and reported thicker, faster-growing hair in the 3% group without a rise in plasma IGF-1 or liver enzymes, as relayed on the HairLossTalk forum. [2][4] Reviewers note that most evidence is preclinical and that topical IGF-1 has a short half-life and low skin permeability. [2]

chain: Liposomes carry IGF-1 into the scalp
IGF-1 signals dermal papilla cells and extends the growth phase
angle.text: The idea is to restore a growth signal that is lower in dermal papilla cells of thinning scalps, using a liposomal gel to help the protein reach the follicle. Animal studies have reported thicker hair; human data on this format are limited. [2][4]

infobox: Hair follicle dermal papilla, IGF-1 receptor [2]
Not an approved hair treatment; mecasermin is an injectable IGF-1 analogue approved for severe IGF-1 deficiency in children [3]

paras: Dermal papilla cells mainly secrete IGF-1, which binds IGF-1 receptor and activates PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK pathways that promote follicular cell proliferation, inhibit apoptosis and push follicles into the anagen phase. [2] IGF-1 raises VEGF expression, supporting angiogenesis and nutrient delivery, and appears to dampen TGF-beta1, a known inhibitor of hair growth. [2] The review links lower IGF-1 and VEGF in androgenetic alopecia to androgens such as DHT. [2]

Because IGF-1 has a short half-life and low skin permeability, topical IGF-1 has been tested mainly as liposomal gels, which showed improved penetration and hair density or thickness in animal and some human reports. [2] Proposed improvements include fusion proteins with Fc, albumin or transferrin and plant-derived exosomes. [2]

The 2025 review says topical IGF-1 showed no systemic toxicity in animals and did not raise circulating IGF-1; clinical safety evidence it cites comes mainly from hearing-loss trials rather than hair studies. [2] Systemic IGF-1 therapy for growth hormone insensitivity has caused transient effects such as hypoglycemia and facial coarsening, with a few benign and malignant tumours reported as treatment-emergent events but too few for risk estimates. [2] Wikipedia notes that high IGF-1 levels are associated with cancer in observational data, while both high and low levels raise mortality risk. [3] Several authors of the review disclose ties to Schweitzer Biotech Company. [2]

Topical IGF-1 has been tested outside hair: a randomized trial in the middle ear used IGF-1-impregnated gelatin hydrogels for sudden deafness refractory to corticosteroids. [5][6] That work concerns hearing rather than hair.

No studies found of a liposomal IGF-1 scalp product in a published human trial. The 2025 review summarises mouse, hamster and rabbit studies and cultured human follicle experiments, including 1994 work in which IGF-1 elongated cultured human follicles in a dose-dependent way, [2] and mentions limited clinical data. A registered 2026 trial compares a scalp elixir with 5% minoxidil in 40 people with hair loss, though it does not specify IGF-1. [7]

timeline.event: Philpott and colleagues report dose-dependent elongation of cultured human follicles with IGF-1. [2]
Hamster study of liposomal IGF-1 gels for hair growth and safety. [2][4]
Review of IGF-1 in hair regeneration published in Current Issues in Molecular Biology. [1][2]

lore.intro: Liposomal IGF-1 is discussed on hair-loss forums mostly through the 2012 hamster abstract rather than through reported personal results. [4]

claims.claim: Liposomal IGF-1 gel regrows hair safely
claims.believers: A forum poster shared the hamster abstract, which concluded the liposomal gel is safe and efficient for hair loss. [4]
claims.experts: A 2025 review says most evidence is animal and in vitro, with limited clinical data and low skin permeability of IGF-1. [2]
